options.text: Bond enthalpy, since C-F is the strongest bond
options.explanation: That factor argues fluoroalkanes are slowest.

options.text: Molar mass, since fluorine is lightest
options.explanation: Mass is not the deciding factor here.

options.text: Atomic radius, since fluorine is smallest
options.explanation: Radius feeds polarity, but the stated factor is the polarity consequence.

questions.stem: Why does the polarity prediction fail?

options.explanation: Nucleophiles seek polar bonds' d+ carbons.

options.text: Bond strength is the greater factor: strong C-F resists breaking despite its polarity
options.explanation: The rate is set by how easily the bond breaks, not how polar it is.

questions.stem: Which order does bond strength give for halogenoalkane reactivity?

options.explanation: Bond enthalpy, falling from C-F to C-I, sets the order.

questions.stem: State the two factors affecting halogenoalkane reactivity.
questions.modelAnswer: Bond polarity (suggesting fluorine fastest) and bond strength (the greater factor, making iodine fastest).

questions.stem: State the direction of the polarity trend down the halogen series.
questions.modelAnswer: Bond polarity decreases from C-F to C-I as electronegativity falls.

questions.stem: Explain why the C-F bond's polarity does not make fluoroalkanes reactive.
questions.modelAnswer: Although the bond is strongly polarised, its very high bond enthalpy means nucleophiles cannot break it, so strength overrides polarity in setting the rate.

questions.stem: A student predicts fluoroalkanes react fastest 'because carbon is most positive there'. Write the correction.
questions.modelAnswer: The d+ carbon does attract nucleophiles, but the rate depends on breaking the C-X bond; C-F is the strongest carbon-halogen bond, so fluoroalkanes are actually the least reactive.

questions.stem: Which carbon-halogen bond is the weakest?

options.explanation: The bond enthalpies differ substantially.

options.text: C-I, requiring the least energy to break
options.explanation: Iodine's large, long bond surrenders its pair most easily.
C-F is the strongest, not the weakest.
Chloride middles the ladder.

options.explanation: The physics of the rate-determining break decides.

questions.stem: State the bond-enthalpy order for the carbon-halogen series.
questions.modelAnswer: C-F strongest, then C-Cl, C-Br, with C-I the weakest.

questions.stem: Write the substitution equation for iodoethane with hydroxide.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3CH2I + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + I-, the fastest hydrolysis of the series.

questions.stem: Explain why iodoalkanes react fastest with nucleophiles.
questions.modelAnswer: The C-I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy, so the rate-determining break happens soonest, liberating iodide and completing substitution fastest.

questions.stem: Predict which halogenoalkane hydrolyses fastest among C2H5Cl, C2H5Br and C2H5I, and justify without naming bond enthalpies.
questions.modelAnswer: C2H5I: iodine is the largest halogen, its bond to carbon is longest and easiest to break, so the iodoalkane surrenders its halide first.
